title: Polynomial accuracy dependence for sublinear LIS estimation
formal: Is there a uniform randomized algorithm which, for every array \(a\in\mathbb R^n\) accessible by adaptive random-access queries and every rational \(0<\varepsilon\le1/2\), returns an estimate \(\widehat L\) with \(\Pr[|\widehat L-\operatorname{LIS}(a)|\le\varepsilon n]\ge2/3\) in \(C(\log(2+n))^c\varepsilon^{-c}\) total operations, for absolute constants C,c? Here LIS uses nondecreasing values.
definitions:
A subsequence is a list of indices \(1\le i_1<\cdots<i_r\le n\). It is increasing in the source convention when \(a_{i_1}\le\cdots\le a_{i_r}\), so equal values are allowed. \(\operatorname{LIS}(a)\) is the largest possible length r, between one and n for nonempty arrays. The algorithm outputs a numerical estimate, not the subsequence itself.

The array is read-only and not preprocessed. An indexed query i returns \(a_i\) at unit cost; later query indices may depend on earlier returned values. Values are exact ordered atoms, permitting constant-time comparisons, and ordinary indices and counters are words of \(O(\log(n/\varepsilon))\) bits. Word arithmetic, comparisons, random bits and memory access are charged. The total operation bound includes computation as well as oracle queries. The accuracy is supplied with \(O(\log(1/\varepsilon))\)-bit rational representation; an equivalent dyadic precision within a constant factor suffices.

The input is arbitrary and fixed; probability is only over the algorithm's coins. The bound is worst-case over inputs and random tapes. Its exponent is uniform in accuracy. A running time with a factor \((1/\varepsilon)^{O(1/\varepsilon)}\), though polylogarithmic in n for fixed accuracy, is not polynomial in inverse accuracy. When the allowed budget exceeds n, reading the array is permitted; no uniformly sublinear requirement is added for very small accuracy.

This is additive error in subsequence length, not a relative approximation when the true LIS is short. Strictly increasing subsequences form a closely related convention, but the present card follows the weak inequality in the checked Saks–Seshadhri source.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked algorithm with the stated uniform total-time and probability guarantees, or its logical negation in this adaptive model. A nonadaptive lower bound alone cannot refute the target. A multiplicative approximation with a growing factor, or polylogarithmic time only for each fixed accuracy with a superpolynomial accuracy dependence, is insufficient.
context:
Saks and Seshadhri obtain additive accuracy with time polylogarithmic in array length, but their bound has a superpolynomial dependence on inverse accuracy. Their definition uses nondecreasing subsequences.

Newman and Varma study different sublinear tradeoffs and nonadaptive lower bounds. These must retain their access restriction when compared to the adaptive target here.
why: This tests whether global order can be estimated with efficient dependence on both input length and accuracy.

import_provenance.original_title: Polynomial accuracy dependence for sublinear LIS estimation
import_provenance.original_statement: With adaptive random access to an array of length n, can its longest increasing subsequence length be estimated to additive error εn in time polynomial in log n and 1/ε? Saks and Seshadhri achieved polylogarithmic dependence on n but exponential dependence on inverse accuracy.
import_provenance.supplied_caveat: Remark: This is an editorial continuation of Saks–Seshadhri. Adaptivity is essential: known nonadaptive lower bounds rule out the stated polynomial dependence simultaneously on log n and 1/ε.

sentences: An algorithm queries entries of an arbitrary ordered array without reading it in full.
It must estimate the longest nondecreasing subsequence length to additive εn error.
The desired total time is polynomial jointly in log n and inverse accuracy.
The classical polylogarithmic-time result has a larger dependence on accuracy.
The target asks whether high-accuracy global order can be estimated efficiently from adaptive local access.
